item.body:
## TL;DR

`cubemastercli tpl create-from-image` timing out (typical errors: `Receive event timeout` or `connection refused` against the probe port) almost always falls into one of two buckets:

1. **Your custom image does not ship `envd`, or `envd` isn't started at container startup.** Cube talks to every sandbox through `envd` — readiness probe, command execution, file I/O all go through it. Without `envd` listening, the readiness probe gets `connection refused` until it times out. **Before building your image, please read: [Bring Your Own Image (envd)](https://cubesandbox.com/guide/tutorials/bring-your-own-image.html).**
2. **You are deploying on AWS EC2 (or any other nested-virtualization environment).** In nested virt:
   - cloud-hypervisor's MicroVM can panic on startup because the host trims the visible instruction set (notably the **XSAVE family**);
   - even when it boots, doubled VM-exits on page faults make the in-guest agent take ~18s to come up (#94), which trips cubemaster/shim's default probe and handshake timeouts.
   - **Fix: switch to PVM deployment** to avoid nested virt altogether.

Details below.

## Typical symptoms

```
failed to create shim task: Others("Other: Create sandbox failed: Receive event timeout after 10000ms")
```

or:

```
Get "http://<sandbox-ip>:49983/health": dial tcp ... connect: connection refused
```

`cubemastercli tpl watch` usually stalls at `phase: CREATING_TEMPLATE` and then transitions to `FAILED`.

---

## Cause 1 — Custom image is missing `envd` or doesn't start it

By default `tpl create-from-image` probes the port `envd` listens on (`49983`) inside the image. Cube waits for `GET :49983/health` to become healthy before taking the template snapshot. If your image:

- doesn't have `envd` installed, or
- has `envd` installed but the `ENTRYPOINT` / `CMD` never starts it,

then the probe keeps getting `connection refused` until cubemaster's probe budget (default 30 s, see #95) is exhausted, and template creation fails with a timeout.

### Fix

Please read the official tutorial first: **[Bring Your Own Image (envd) — cubesandbox.com](https://cubesandbox.com/guide/tutorials/bring-your-own-image.html)**

It covers, in detail:

- Why Cube needs `envd` (and which SDK capabilities depend on it)
- Recommended path 1: build on top of the official `cubesandbox-base` image (easiest)
- Recommended path 2: use `COPY --from=` to inject `envd` into your existing image
- The `cube-entrypoint.sh` contract (how to run `envd` in the background while keeping your own `CMD` in the foreground)
- How to verify the image locally with `docker run` + `curl :49983/health`

Once your image follows that contract, re-run `cubemastercli tpl create-from-image`. In ~99% of "custom image" cases the timeout simply goes away.

---

## Cause 2 — Deploying on AWS EC2 (or another nested-virt environment)

AWS EC2's nested virtualization exposes a heavily trimmed instruction set to guests. Cube's default deployment relies on cloud-hypervisor to launch the MicroVM, and runs into two recurring problems:

- **Missing XSAVE family** → cloud-hypervisor's MicroVM panics on startup. From the outside this looks like `Receive event timeout` — template creation fails 100% of the time.
- **Slow nested startup** → even when the MicroVM does come up, doubled VM-exits on page faults stretch the in-guest agent's startup to ~18 s, blowing the shim-side `VsockServerReady` timeout (#94) and the cubemastercli-side probe budget (#95).
- Even if you stretch the timeouts enough to "succeed", **the resulting sandboxes are slow** — not a reasonable production or benchmarking setup.

### Fix: switch to PVM deployment

PVM runs the guest directly on top of the host kernel, **without depending on nested KVM**, which dodges both the missing-XSAVE panic and the slow-nested-startup problem in one shot.

- Docs: [PVM Deployment](https://cubesandbox.com/guide/pvm-deploy.html)
- On AWS Amazon Linux 2023 the PVM kernel has a few distro-specific installation gotchas (e.g. `rpm -ivh` trips on `kernel-headers obsoleted`; use `dnf install --allowerasing` instead) — see #161 for the install notes.

### What if I'm already on nested virt and can't move to PVM yet?

The short-term workaround is to widen the timeouts, but that only hides the symptom — **the underlying performance and missing-instruction-set problems remain**. We still recommend migrating to PVM as soon as you can.

---

## See also

- #95 — `cubemastercli: default --probe budget of 30s is too tight for slower hosts` (OPEN).
- #94 — `shim: VsockServerReady wait of 10s is too tight for nested-KVM hosts` (CLOSED; ~18 s in-guest agent startup under nested KVM).
- #161 — `[Bug Report] PVM Deployment fails to boot kernel on AWS C8i + Amazon Linux 2023` (OPEN; PVM kernel installation steps for AL2023).
- #253 — `[Bug Report] Template build fails every time` (CLOSED; collection of WSL / VMware / nested cloud-VM repros).

---

If you hit a scenario this FAQ doesn't cover (other clouds' nested virt, exotic container entrypoint shapes, etc.), please leave a comment and we'll fold it in.

item.title: [FAQ] Why does custom template creation (tpl create-from-image) keep timing out?

item.body:
## TL;DR

- `cubelet` stores **container writable layers** under **`/data/cubelet`** and relies on **XFS reflink** to clone them in O(1) time.
- Therefore `/data/cubelet` **must live on an XFS filesystem** with reflink enabled (the `mkfs.xfs` default). Otherwise the `one-click install.sh` pre-flight check refuses to start.
- **Production**: mount a **dedicated XFS data disk** at `/data/cubelet` (we suggest at least **100–300 GiB**).
- **Testing / evaluation**: as a workaround, use a loopback `.img` file formatted as XFS and mounted at `/data/cubelet`.
- **Fresh installs**: prefer **OpenCloudOS 9** or another RHEL-family distro (RHEL 9 / Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9). Their root filesystem is XFS by default — no extra mount steps needed.

## Affected scenarios

Ubuntu / Debian-family distros ship with an ext4 root filesystem. When deploying on the whole machine without a dedicated data disk, `/data/cubelet` ends up under `/`, and the one-click pre-flight check refuses to proceed:

```
[one-click] ERROR: The filesystem that will host /data/cubelet is on '/' (type: ext4), which is not XFS.
  Cube Sandbox requires the /data/cubelet directory to reside on an XFS filesystem.
  Options:
    1. Mount a dedicated XFS-formatted partition at /data/cubelet:
         mkfs.xfs /dev/<your-partition>
         mount /dev/<your-partition> /data/cubelet
    2. Ensure the parent path (/) itself is on XFS.
```

WSL and most cloud VMs also default to ext4, so this is a very common situation.

## Why XFS?

`cubelet` clones every sandbox's writable layer with `cp --reflink=always <base> <target>` against a shared base ext4 image, in **O(1) wall time**. `--reflink=always` requires kernel-level **CoW block sharing** via the `FICLONE` ioctl from the **underlying filesystem**.

On Linux, the filesystem we officially support and exercise on the reflink fast path is **XFS (`reflink=1`)**. **ext4 does not implement `FICLONE`**, so placing `/data/cubelet` on ext4 prevents cubelet from taking the fast path — hence the pre-flight refuses up front.

## Recommended setups

### Option A — Dedicated XFS data disk (recommended for production)

Best performance and isolation. `/data/cubelet` stores both template artifacts and per-sandbox writable layers, so plan for **at least 100–300 GiB**.

```bash
# Assume /dev/vdb is the data disk
sudo mkfs.xfs -f /dev/vdb
sudo mkdir -p /data/cubelet
echo "/dev/vdb /data/cubelet xfs defaults 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo mount -a

# Verify reflink is enabled (the output should contain reflink=1)
xfs_info /data/cubelet | grep reflink
```

### Option B — Loopback file + XFS (workaround for testing / evaluation)

When no dedicated data disk is available (laptops, single-disk cloud VMs, WSL), use a sparse `.img` file plus a loop mount.

```bash
# 1) Create a 100 GiB sparse img file
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/cubelet-loop
sudo truncate -s 100G /var/lib/cubelet-loop/cubelet.img

# 2) Format it as XFS
sudo mkfs.xfs /var/lib/cubelet-loop/cubelet.img

# 3) Mount it at /data/cubelet
sudo mkdir -p /data/cubelet
sudo mount -o loop /var/lib/cubelet-loop/cubelet.img /data/cubelet

# 4) Persist via /etc/fstab
echo "/var/lib/cubelet-loop/cubelet.img /data/cubelet xfs loop 0 0" \
  | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

# 5) Verify reflink is enabled
xfs_info /data/cubelet | grep reflink
```

> ⚠️ The loopback file itself still lives on the underlying ext4 — that adds another I/O hop. **Use this only for testing / evaluation.** For production, please use Option A.

### Option C — Pick a distro with XFS by default (recommended for fresh installs)

If the host has not been provisioned yet and you have OS freedom, just pick a distro whose root filesystem is already XFS — no mount gymnastics required:

- **OpenCloudOS 9** (preferred)
- Other RHEL-family distros: RHEL 9 / Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9 / CentOS Stream 9

On these distros, even without a dedicated data disk, `/data/cubelet` sitting under `/` passes the pre-flight check. You can still attach a dedicated XFS data disk later per Option A if you need more headroom or isolation.

## See also

- #245 — Original bug report: Ubuntu 22.04 self-build deployment, one-click rejects with `not XFS`. This FAQ is the canonical answer for that issue.
- #235 — A separate concurrency-time reflink issue that surfaces *after* `/data/cubelet` is already XFS (closed; linked here as related reflink history).

---

If you hit a scenario this FAQ doesn't cover (specific cloud vendor, exotic storage backend, etc.), please leave a comment below and we'll fold it in.

## Summary

Template creation (`cubemastercli tpl create-from-image`) **fails on v0.2.1** but **succeeds on v0.2.0** on the same bare-metal host — appears to be a regression introduced in v0.2.1.

## Environment

- Bare-metal server, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, x86_64
- Native KVM: `/dev/kvm` present, CPU has `vmx`, `kvm_intel` nested=Y, `systemd-detect-virt` = `none`
- 40 vCPU / 62 GB RAM
- `/data/cubelet` on a dedicated XFS filesystem (`reflink=1`)
- Install: one-click `online-install.sh` with `MIRROR=cn`

## v0.2.1 (`cube-sandbox-one-click-6894862`) — FAILS

`cubemastercli tpl create-from-image --image .../cube-sandbox/sandbox-code:latest` fails. Two modes:

1. First run — fails in **DISTRIBUTING**:
   `rpc error: code = Unimplemented desc = unknown service cubelet.services.images.v1.Images`
   (worked around by re-running `scripts/one-click/up.sh`)

2. After a clean restart — progresses to **CREATING_TEMPLATE (85%)**, then fails:
   `cubelet create image rfs-... failed: pull image rfs-...: ensure pmem file failed: target kernel file /usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/cubebox_os_image/rfs-.../rfs-....vm not exist`

On startup, `cubelet.log` emits many warnings:

```
Ignoring unknown key in TOML for plugin  error="strict mode: fields in the document are missing in the target struct"  key=<KEY>  plugin=io.cubelet.internal.v1.network
```

for keys: `object_dir`, `redis_conf_path`, `tap_init_num`, `watch_stream`, `mvm_inner_ip`, `mvm_mac_addr`, `stream_key`, `stream_name_prefix`, `report_stat_interval_in_sec`, ... — suggesting the `cubelet` binary and the network-plugin config schema shipped in the v0.2.1 one-click bundle are out of sync.

## v0.2.0 (`cube-sandbox-one-click-9c16021`) — WORKS

Same host, same install method (`MIRROR=cn`), same `tpl create-from-image` command: the template reaches **READY** (`distribution: 1/1 ready, 0 failed`). Sandbox creation, `run_code`, `commands.run`, and filesystem read/write via the E2B SDK all work correctly.

## Suspected cause

The v0.2.1 release notes mention *"Skip SHA256 on every startup — split kernel file operations"*. The failure (`target kernel file ....vm not exist`) is in exactly that code path. May also be a regression of the (closed) template-creation issues #251 / #253.

## Ask

- Is this a known v0.2.1 regression?
- Is staying on v0.2.0 the recommended workaround, or is a fix planned?

Thanks for open-sourcing CubeSandbox — happy to provide full logs.

item.body:
####  Motivation
CubeSandbox currently relies on `ext4` for Rootfs and Guest OS images. However, `ext4` is not the most efficient choice for read-only, high-density AI sandbox environments. It leads to larger image sizes and suboptimal IO performance during massive concurrent cold starts.

#### Proposed Solution
Support **EROFS (Enhanced Read-Only File System)** as a modern alternative to `ext4` to achieve:
*   **Reduced Image Size**: Leverage transparent compression (LZ4) to significantly cut down distribution bandwidth and storage overhead.
*   **Performance Optimization**: Faster metadata lookups and lower IO latency during high-concurrency cold starts.
*   **Native Integrity**: A natively immutable filesystem that provides better security for read-only Rootfs.

#### Proposed Implementation
*   **CubeMaster**: Integrate `mkfs.erofs` into the image building pipeline and update metadata to support EROFS media type.
*   **Cubelet**: Remove the hardcoded block for EROFS and support dynamic `FsType` for pmem devices.
*   **CubeShim**: Allow `rootfstype=erofs` in the VM boot configuration.

#### Additional Context
This alignment follows industry best practices for container runtimes, similar to the work being done in Kata Containers: [kata-containers/pull/13019](https://github.com/kata-containers/kata-containers/pull/13019).
> The NVIDIA images go down from 1.2GB to less than 500MB.

comments.body: I think this issue may be related to the insufficient size of your ext4 image

Hi @woshihoujinxin,

After further investigation, we've confirmed that the root cause of this issue is **insufficient disk space on the system partition** (where `/tmp` resides). When creating the ext4 filesystem, `mkfs.ext4` uses a temporary directory under `/tmp` to stage artifacts, and if the root partition runs out of space during this process, it results in the checksum/inode errors you observed — which can be misleading.

To resolve this, please ensure your system partition has enough free space. Alternatively, you can configure the artifact directory to use a different partition with more space by setting the `CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR` environment variable.

Closing this issue as the root cause is environmental. Feel free to reopen if the problem persists after freeing up disk space.

# Bug: CubeSandbox 模版创建失败 - mkfs.ext4 文件系统错误

## 摘要

CubeSandbox 在从包含 OpenViking 的 OCI 镜像创建模版时，mkfs.ext4 阶段失败。错误表现为两种形式：
1. "Directory block checksum does not match" - 校验和不匹配
2. "Ext2 inode is not a directory" - inode 类型冲突

**问题已确认可复现**，使用官方 openclaw 镜像 + OpenViking 组合。

## 环境信息

| 项目 | 版本 |
|------|------|
| **CubeSandbox** | PVM 模式 |
| **内核** | 6.6.69-cube.pvm.host.005.x-gb85200d80fa2 |
| **基础镜像** | ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.3.8 |
| **OpenViking** | 0.3.3 |
| **文件系统** | /data/cubelet (xfs), / (ext4) |
| **mkfs.ext4** | mke2fs 1.46.5 |

## 错误信息

### 错误类型 1: 校验和不匹配

```
error: mkfs.ext4 failed: exit status 1: mke2fs 1.46.5 (30-Dec-2021)
Discarding device blocks:       0/2097152done                            
Creating filesystem with 2097152 4k blocks and 524288 inodes
...
Copying files into the device: libggml-base.so: Directory block checksum does not match directory block while looking up "libggml-base.so"
mkfs.ext4: Directory block checksum does not match directory block while populating file system
```

### 错误类型 2: inode 类型冲突

```
error: mkfs.ext4 failed: exit status 1: mke2fs 1.46.5 (30-Dec-2021)
Discarding device blocks:       0/1048576done                            
Creating filesystem with 1048576 4k blocks and 262144 inodes
...
Copying files into the device: _better_exceptions.py: Ext2 inode is not a directory while looking up "_better_exceptions.py"
mkfs.ext4: Ext2 inode is not a directory while populating file system
```

## 复现步骤

### 1. 创建测试 Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# 
# 用途：复现 CubeSandbox 模版创建时的 mkfs.ext4 错误
# 构建：docker build -t openclaw-openviking-test .
# ==============================================================================

# Stage 1: 构建 openviking-plugin
FROM m.daocloud.io/docker.io/node:22-alpine AS openviking-builder

WORKDIR /build/openviking-plugin

# 从 GitHub 官方仓库下载 OpenViking 源码
RUN wget https://github.com/volcengine/OpenViking/archive/refs/tags/v0.3.3.tar.gz -O OpenViking-0.3.3.tar.gz

RUN tar -xzf OpenViking-0.3.3.tar.gz -C /tmp/ && \
    cp -r /tmp/OpenViking-0.3.3/examples/openclaw-plugin/. . && \
    rm -rf /tmp/OpenViking-0.3.3 OpenViking-0.3.3.tar.gz && \
    npm install --no-audit --no-fund --registry https://registry.npmmirror.com

# Stage 2: 最终镜像
FROM ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.3.8

USER root

# 替换为阿里云源（加速构建）
RUN rm -f /etc/apt/sources.list.d/debian.sources && \
    echo "deb http://mirrors.aliyun.com/debian bookworm main contrib non-free non-free-firmware" > /etc/apt/sources.list && \
    echo "deb http://mirrors.aliyun.com/debian bookworm-updates main contrib non-free non-free-firmware" >> /etc/apt/sources.list && \
    echo "deb http://mirrors.aliyun.com/debian-security bookworm-security main contrib non-free non-free-firmware" >> /etc/apt/sources.list

# 安装 Python 和 pip
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y python3-pip && \
    apt-get clean && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# 安装 openviking==0.3.3（包含 @node-llama-cpp 依赖）
RUN pip3 install --no-cache-dir --break-system-packages \
    -i https://mirrors.aliyun.com/pypi/simple/ \
    --trusted-host mirrors.aliyun.com \
    openviking==0.3.3

# 安装 openviking-plugin
RUN mkdir -p /opt/openclaw-extensions/openviking
COPY --from=openviking-builder /build/openviking-plugin/ /opt/openclaw-extensions/openviking/

RUN chown -R 1000:1000 /opt/openclaw-extensions

# 清理 .pyc 文件
RUN find / -type f -name "*.pyc" -delete 2>/dev/null || true && \
    find / -type d -name "__pycache__" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null || true

USER 1000

ENTRYPOINT ["node", "openclaw.mjs", "gateway", "--allow-unconfigured"]
```

### 2. 构建镜像

```bash
docker build -f Dockerfile.openviking-test \
  -t your-registry/openclaw:openviking-test .
```

### 3. 创建模版

```bash
cubemastercli tpl create-from-image \
    --image your-registry/openclaw:openviking-test \
    --writable-layer-size 1G
```

### 4. 观察结果

模版创建在 **BUILDING_EXT4** 阶段失败，错误信息如上所示。

## 根本原因分析

### 问题来源

OpenViking 包含 `@node-llama-cpp` 依赖，该依赖包含大量 native 共享库文件：
- `libggml-base.so` (738KB)
- `libggml-cpu-*.so` (多个 CPU 变体)
- `libggml-cuda.so` (CUDA 版本)
- `libggml-vulkan.so` (Vulkan 版本)
- 总计 60+ 个 .so 文件

### mkfs.ext4 复制文件机制

mkfs.ext4 在创建文件系统时：
1. 创建 ext4 文件系统结构
2. 遍历源目录复制文件
3. 为每个文件计算 inode 和数据块校验和
4. 将校验和写入目录块

**当文件具有特殊属性时**（如某些 native 共享库），校验和计算可能出现不一致。

### 为什么有两种错误？

| 错误类型 | 触发条件 |
|---------|---------|
| Directory block checksum | 文件内容校验和不匹配 |
| Ext2 inode is not a directory | inode 类型与文件类型冲突 |

这说明问题不是特定于某个文件，而是 **mkfs.ext4 与某些文件结构不兼容的通用问题**。

## 已尝试的解决方案

| 方案 | 效果 | 局限 |
|------|------|------|
| `--no-bin-links` | 解决符号链接问题 | 无法解决 .so 文件 |
| 清理 .pyc 文件 | 解决 Python 缓存问题 | 无法解决 .so 文件 |
| 移除 OpenViking | ✅ 完全解决 | 失去长期记忆功能 |

## 建议的解决方案

### 短期方案（用户侧）

1. **不使用 OpenViking** - 移除相关依赖
2. **使用其他长期记忆方案** - 如外部向量数据库

### 长期方案（产品侧）

1. **改进错误提示**
   ```bash
   # 在模版创建前检测潜在问题文件
   cubemastercli tpl create-from-image \
       --dry-run \  # 预检查模式
       --image <image>
   ```

2. **添加文件系统选项**
   ```bash
   # 支持不同的文件系统格式
   cubemastercli tpl create-from-image \
       --fs-type squashfs \  # 或其他格式
       --image <image>
   ```

3. **增强 tpl status 输出**
   ```
   - 显示模版存放路径
   - 显示当前正在处理的文件
   - 显示临时文件大小
   ```

## 影响范围

- ✅ **官方 openclaw 镜像** - 模版创建成功
- ❌ **openclaw + OpenViking** - 模版创建失败
- ✅ **移除 OpenViking 的自定义镜像** - 模版创建成功

## 参考

- **模版 ID**: tpl-280d49201ddf40fdbc2f4382 (失败), tpl-35b73b468a0146aa9c88a299 (成功)
- **测试镜像**: hub-vpc-cn-beijing-6.kce.ksyun.com/dcf_dev/openclaw:openviking-test
- **相关 Issue**: issue-template-dir-space.md (根分区空间问题)
- **内核版本**: 6.6.69-cube.pvm.host.005.x-gb85200d80fa2

# Issue: 临时目录空间不足导致模版构建失败

## 问题描述

CubeSandbox 在从 OCI 镜像创建模版时，模版创建进度卡在 `UNPACKING` 20% 左右，最终超时失败。

## 环境信息

- 磁盘布局：
  - 根分区 `/dev/vda2`: 50G，系统占用后仅剩 ~5G 空闲
  - 数据分区 `/dev/vdb`: 200G，挂载至 `/data/cubelet`，有 ~150G 空闲

## 根本原因

### 1. 临时工作目录默认在根分区

CubeSandbox (cubemaster) 在创建模版时需要大量临时空间用于：
- 镜像解压
- rootfs 构建
- ext4 文件系统创建

默认情况下，临时工作目录 `CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR` 为 `/tmp/cubemaster-rootfs-artifacts/`，位于根分区。

### 2. 空间需求

对于一个 1.6GB 的 OCI 镜像，模版创建过程大约需要 8-10GB 的临时空间：
- 镜像层解压
- 中间文件
- ext4 镜像构建

根分区仅剩 5GB 空间，无法满足需求。

## 解决方案

### 修改启动脚本 `/usr/local/services/cubetoolbox/scripts/one-click/up.sh`

添加 `CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR` 环境变量，将临时工作目录指向大分区：

```bash
# 新增：临时工作目录配置
CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR_DEFAULT="/data/cubelet/tmp/cubemaster-rootfs-artifacts"
CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR_CONFIGURED="${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR:-}"
CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR="${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR_CONFIGURED:-${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR_DEFAULT}}"

# 配置临时工作目录（大分区）
if [[ -n "${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR_CONFIGURED}" ]]; then
  mkdir -p "${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR}"
  CUBEMASTER_ARTIFACT_DIR_EXPORT="export CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR=\"${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR}\";"
elif mkdir -p "${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  CUBEMASTER_ARTIFACT_DIR_EXPORT="export CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR=\"${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR}\";"
else
  log "cubemaster artifact work dir ${CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR} unavailable, using /tmp fallback"
fi

# 启动时传递环境变量
start_with_pidfile \
  "cubemaster" \
  "export CUBE_MASTER_CONFIG_PATH=\"${CUBEMASTER_CFG}\"; ${CUBEMASTER_ARTIFACT_STORE_EXPORT} ${CUBEMASTER_ARTIFACT_DIR_EXPORT} \"${CUBEMASTER_BIN}\""
```

## 环境变量说明

| 变量 | 用途 | 默认值 | 建议值 |
|------|------|--------|--------|
| `CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR` | 临时工作目录 | `/tmp/cubemaster-rootfs-artifacts` | `/data/cubelet/tmp/cubemaster-rootfs-artifacts` |
| `CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_STORE_DIR` | 最终存储目录 | `/data/CubeMaster/storage` | `/data/CubeMaster/storage` |

## 建议改进

1. **文档更新**: 在部署文档中明确说明磁盘空间要求，建议根分区至少保留 20GB 空闲空间

2. **默认配置优化**: 建议官方安装脚本/配置默认将临时目录设置到大分区

3. **空间检查**: 在模版创建前检查临时目录可用空间，不足时提前报错而非卡住

4. **清理机制**: 添加失败模版的临时文件自动清理机制

## 验证方法

```bash
# 1. 检查环境变量是否生效
cat /proc/<cubemaster-pid>/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | grep CUBEMASTER_ROOTFS_ARTIFACT_DIR

# 2. 监控临时目录使用情况
watch -n 5 'du -sh /data/cubelet/tmp/cubemaster-rootfs-artifacts/*'

# 3. 检查模版创建进度
cubemastercli tpl ls
```

Hi, I'm trying the `host-mount` example and found a permission issue when writing to a mounted host directory.

### Reproduction

Host directory:

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/rw
```

The directory is created by my normal host user:

```bash
$ id lzx
uid=1002(lzx) gid=1002(lzx)
```

Python example:

```python
import json
import os
from e2b_code_interpreter import Sandbox
from env_utils import load_local_dotenv

load_local_dotenv()
template_id = os.environ["CUBE_TEMPLATE_ID"]

with Sandbox.create(
    template=template_id,
    metadata={
        "host-mount": json.dumps([
            {
                "hostPath":  "/tmp/rw",
                "mountPath": "/mnt/rw",
                "readOnly":  False,
            },
        ])
    },
) as sandbox:
    result = sandbox.commands.run("echo hello world > /mnt/rw/1.txt")
```

### Actual behavior

The command fails with:

```text
e2b.sandbox.commands.command_handle.CommandExitException:
Command exited with code 1 and error:

/bin/bash: line 1: /mnt/rw/1.txt: Permission denied
```

### Root cause analysis

The issue seems to be caused by UID mismatch:

* Host directory owner:

  * `lzx` (`uid=1002`)
* Sandbox default user:

  * `user` (`uid=1000`)

Since the mounted directory keeps the original host ownership and permissions, the sandbox user cannot write to it.

### Questions

I'm wondering what the recommended / intended behavior should be here.

Possible solutions I can think of:

1. Manually `chown` the host directory to match sandbox UID/GID

```bash
sudo chown -R 1000:1000 /tmp/rw
```

2. Run commands as root inside the sandbox

```python
sandbox.commands.run(..., user="root")
```

3. Automatically remap ownership / permissions during mount

For example:

* UID/GID mapping
* user namespace remapping
* mount-time ownership adjustment

### Discussion

At the moment, the current behavior is understandable from a Linux mount/permission perspective, but it may be surprising for users because the example appears to support read-write mounts out of the box.

So I’m not sure whether:

* this is expected usage and should be documented more clearly,
* or whether this is considered a UX/design issue that should be improved inside CubeSandbox itself.

Would appreciate guidance on the recommended best practice here.
Good point， I think we can have better documentation here on the host machine directory permissions, guiding on how to reasonably set the directory permissions of the host machine

## Environment

- CubeSandbox v0.2.0 via official one-click installer (`cube-sandbox-one-click-9c16021/install.sh`)
- Host: bare-metal Intel i7-12700, Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 6.14
- `/data/cubelet` on XFS with `reflink=1` (verified via `xfs_info`), 30 GiB free
- `PoolType: cp_reflink_type` (probe in `checkPoolType` succeeded, so cubelet stayed on the reflink path)
- Template: `python:3.12-slim`, `--writable-layer-size 2Gi`

## Repro

```bash
# 1. Template
cubemastercli template create-from-image \
    --image python:3.12-slim \
    --template-id repro-pynp \
    --writable-layer-size 2Gi \
    --allow-internet-access

# 2. Fire 100 concurrent POST /sandboxes against cube-api,
#    then DELETE each on success.
```

## Observed

- Run A: **77/100** sandboxes spawned cleanly, wall-clock 20.3 s.
- Run B: **36/100** spawned cleanly, wall-clock 19.8 s.

Wall-clock is stable across runs; success rate is variable. Failed spawns log:

```
newExt4RawByReflinkCopy failed: e2fsck 1.47.0 (5-Feb-2023):
bad magic number in superblock
```

Variable success rate + stable wall-clock suggests a timing-sensitive
concurrency issue rather than a deterministic config problem.

## Analysis

I read `Cubelet/storage/{shell.go, pool.go, plugin.go}`. A few observations
that may be relevant — happy to PR fixes for the mechanical ones if you
agree on direction.

### 1. `cmdTimeout = 3 * time.Second` may be too short for multi-GiB ext4 ops

[`shell.go`](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/blob/master/Cubelet/storage/shell.go) defines:

```go
const cmdTimeout = time.Second * 3
```

`newExt4RawByReflinkCopy` runs four commands under this single timeout:

```
cp --reflink=always base target
truncate -s <newsize> target
e2fsck -fy target
resize2fs target
```

For `--writable-layer-size 2Gi`, `target` is truncated to ~3 GiB. Under
N=100 concurrent invocations sharing one XFS volume, `e2fsck -fy` and
`resize2fs` on a 3 GiB image can plausibly exceed 3 s. When the timeout
fires, `utils.ExecV` terminates the in-flight process and the target file
is left in a half-finished state — which would explain the next
command reading a missing/corrupted superblock.

### 2. Per-clone `e2fsck` is the most likely failure window, and may be removable

`target` is cloned from a freshly `mkfs.ext4`'d base that has never been
mounted-and-written. Its superblock is byte-identical to the base by
construction. Per-clone `e2fsck` exists, as far as I can tell, only to
satisfy `resize2fs`'s clean-fs requirement — not to catch real
corruption.

Two cleaner shapes:

- `resize2fs -f target` (force, skip the fsck precondition) plus a
  one-time `e2fsck` on the base at pool init.
- Or: create the base at the final per-sandbox size, so the
  truncate+resize step disappears entirely and `cp --reflink` alone
  suffices.

### 3. XFS FICLONE may serialize on the source inode under high concurrency

`cp --reflink=always` issues `FICLONE` on the source. Under N=100
concurrent calls cloning the same base file, kernel-side serialization
on the source inode is plausible and would amplify (1) — the tail of
the cohort experiences higher latency than the head, raising the
probability of hitting `cmdTimeout` on the chained commands.

(I haven't profiled this directly; flagging it as a hypothesis.)

### 4. Error path lacks diagnostic info, making this hard to root-cause

```go
if _, stderr, err = utils.ExecV(cmd, cmdTimeout); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("newExt4RawByReflinkCopy failed:%s", stderr)
}
```

The returned error contains only the failing command's stderr. It
doesn't expose:

- which of the four commands failed (cp / truncate / e2fsck / resize2fs)
- `stat(target)` (is the file 0 bytes? half-extended?)
- `stat(base)` and free disk space on the volume
- elapsed time before the failure

These are all cheap to capture and would dramatically improve future
debuggability.

### 5. Base file is not integrity-checked before reuse

[`newExt4BaseRaw`](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/blob/master/Cubelet/storage/shell.go) short-circuits on:

```go
ok, _ := utils.FileExistAndValid(filePath)
if ok {
    return nil
}
```

If `FileExistAndValid` does not parse the ext4 superblock (I didn't
read its source), a prior cubelet crash mid-`mkfs.ext4` could leave a
half-written base. The next cubelet start would skip recreation and
every clone would fail thereafter. I haven't directly observed this
on our host but the symptom shape is consistent.

## Proposal

If you agree these are real, happy to send the following as separate PRs:

1. **Configurable `cmdTimeout` + default raised to 30 s.** Mechanical, low risk.
2. **Diagnostic-rich error wrap** in `newExt4RawByReflinkCopy`: include
   command index, `stat(target)`, `stat(base)`, free space, elapsed time.
   Pure addition, doesn't change behaviour.
3. **(More invasive — would prefer your input first)** Drop per-clone
   `e2fsck`, add a one-time integrity check on base at pool init, and
   use `resize2fs -f`.

Want to defer to your judgement on (3). (1) and (2) I can ship soon if
you greenlight.

## Disclosure

I ran into this while benchmarking sandbox runtimes for a fork-on-write
project — [forkd](https://github.com/deeplethe/forkd). Not claiming cube
is slow; your advertised \`<60 ms\` single-instance cold-start is faster
than what I'm building. This particular failure mode showed up under
the N=100 concurrent shape and looked worth surfacing whether or not
it's relevant to my benchmark.

Repo with the bench harness I used: [`bench/CUBESANDBOX.md`](https://github.com/deeplethe/forkd/blob/main/bench/CUBESANDBOX.md).

## Summary

Sandbox creation always fails with `open /proc/66/ns/mnt failed: No such file or directory (os error 2)` after PVM snapshot restore. Template creation (cold boot path) works perfectly — only the restore path fails.

## Environment

- **CubeSandbox version**: v0.2.0 (online install)
- **Host OS and kernel version**: CentOS Stream 9 / 6.6.69-cube.pvm.host.005.x-gb85200d80fa2 (also reproduced on Ubuntu 22.04)
- **Guest Kernel**: 6.6.69-cube.pvm.guest.005.x-gb85200d80fa2
- **KVM info**: kvm_pvm module loaded, /dev/kvm available
- **Deployment mode**: single-node
- **Relevant component**: CubeShim / agent (cube_agent)
- **Hardware**: AMD EPYC 9T24, 64 vCPU, 247GB RAM (Alibaba Cloud ECS, no nested virtualization)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install CubeSandbox with `CUBE_PVM_ENABLE=1` on a host without nested virtualization
2. Create a template (e.g., Ubuntu-based) — this succeeds and reaches READY state
3. Attempt to create a sandbox from that template — this always fails

## Expected Behavior

Sandbox should be created successfully from the template snapshot, with the container running inside the restored micro-VM.

## Actual Behavior

Sandbox creation fails at the `CreateContainer` step after `RestoreVm`. The guest agent (`cube_agent`) cannot enter the mount namespace of the container init process because the process no longer exists after snapshot restore.

### cube-shim-stat.log

The pattern is deterministic — cold boot `CreateContainer` always succeeds, restore `CreateContainer` always fails:

```
# Template creation (cold boot) - SUCCESS
test-ubuntu2_0 BootVm 0 82523
test-ubuntu2_0 CreateContainer 0 31    ← SUCCESS (31ms)

# Sandbox creation (restore) - FAIL
sbx-xxx RestoreVm 0 1076
sbx-xxx CreateContainer 1 18           ← FAIL (error code 1, 18ms)
```

### cube-shim-req.log

```
open /proc/66/ns/mnt failed:No such file or directory (os error 2)
```

### VMM log

```
[restore_vm] pvm restore takes Duration { secs: 0, nanos: 865183242 }
```

The VM restore itself completes successfully (sub-second), but the guest process table is not properly preserved.

## Additional Context

### Root Cause Analysis

The `cube_agent` inside the guest VM attempts to enter the mount namespace of the container init process (PID 66) via `/proc/66/ns/mnt`. During cold boot (template creation), this process exists and the operation succeeds. After snapshot restore, PID 66 no longer exists in the guest's `/proc`, causing the mount namespace entry to fail.

This suggests that PVM's snapshot/restore mechanism does not fully preserve the guest process state — specifically, processes that existed at snapshot time are not properly restored, making their `/proc/PID/ns/*` entries unavailable.

### Key Observations

- Tested on both Ubuntu 22.04 and CentOS Stream 9 with identical results
- All PVM kernel parameters are properly set (clearcpuid, pti=off, tsc=reliable, etc.)
- `kvm_pvm` module loads correctly, `/dev/kvm` is available
- Template creation (which uses cold boot) works reliably every time
- Only the snapshot restore → CreateContainer path fails
- The issue is 100% reproducible across multiple templates and sandbox attempts

## Closing as Invalid

After further analysis, this issue is **not a valid bug**:

1. The test case relied on BUG-0006 (CleanUp storm SIGKILLing envd after pause) to create a "dead but record still exists" scenario.
2. **BUG-0006 has been fixed** — paused sandboxes now survive correctly and are not destroyed by DeadGC/CleanUp.
3. With BUG-0006 fixed, `POST /sandboxes/<id>/connect` on a paused sandbox correctly performs **resume** and returns 200. This is the intended behavior.

The original scenario ("envd is dead but connect silently returns 200") can no longer be reproduced because the underlying cause (BUG-0006) no longer kills paused sandboxes.

**Conclusion**: `connect` returning 200 on a paused sandbox = correct resume semantics. Closing as invalid.

## Description

`POST /sandboxes/<id>/connect` returns HTTP 200 with a valid-looking response for sandboxes that are not in a connectable state (e.g., paused but not yet cleaned up, or in a transitional state). This is a "fast-path" in `handlers/sandboxes.rs` that silently succeeds without actually establishing a connection.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a sandbox
2. Pause it
3. Wait for it to enter an intermediate state (paused but Cubelet has not fully acknowledged)
4. Call `POST /sandboxes/<id>/connect`
5. Observe HTTP 200 response even though the sandbox cannot accept connections

## Expected Behavior

Should return an appropriate error:
- `409 Conflict` if sandbox is in a transitional state
- `503 Service Unavailable` if sandbox is not connectable
- At minimum, return a non-2xx status code

## Actual Behavior

Returns HTTP 200 with a response body, giving the client false confidence that a connection was established.

## Impact

- Client SDKs proceed to use the "connection" and encounter cryptic failures later
- Makes sandbox lifecycle state machines unreliable from the client perspective

## Root Cause (suspected)

`handlers/sandboxes.rs` has a fast-path that returns 200 without verifying the sandbox is actually in a connectable state (running with envd ready).

## Environment

- CubeSandbox master branch (2026-05-13)
- Affected component: CubeAPI handlers/sandboxes.rs

comments.body: I think we can put the VMM process in a cgroup and configure the cgroup to meet your requirements. However, for the scenario you described, wouldn't it be more reasonable to utilize the pause/resume capability, pausing during most idle times and resuming when work is needed?

Thanks @kinwin-ustc. Several thoughts on this:

* If pause/resume is only in-place, it helps with idle CPU usage, but it does not reclaim much memory.
* If we rely on pause + snapshot/restore to reclaim memory, then memory/filesystem snapshotting becomes load-bearing. Memory snapshotting especially tends to be finicky.
* It also pushes a lot of correctness into user space
* That might work for some applications, but some state is hard to serialize or resume cleanly, e.g. DB connections, open transactions, sockets, in-flight I/O, credentials, etc.
* There is also a latency concern. CubeSandbox pause takes ~2s in my testing. With rollouts that make ~200 tool calls, pausing after every call would add up quickly. We could be smarter with TTL-based idle pausing and reduce that to maybe 10-20 pause/resume cycles, but tail latencies could still hurt step time.

Our pause-and-resume mechanism saves memory snapshots to disk, conserving both CPU and memory. While external connections, credential refresh, and InFlight I/O do pose challenges for pause-and-resume, these can be mitigated through TTL pausing(Pause after an idle period）and user-space control (e.g., re-establishing connections and refreshing credentials upon resumption). Even with cgroup CPU limiting to restrict CPU consumption in the idle sandbox, idle connection heartbeats and credential refreshes still require handling. Furthermore, for pause-and-resume, the user-perceived time is actually the recovery time; pause time has minimal impact, while recovery can be controlled to the millisecond level.

I agree it can be mitigated but still feel it's useful in some cases. Wondering how hard is it to support it? I chatted with agents on this -- is it basically using cgroup's `cpu.max.burst` API? https://github.com/vwxyzjn/CubeSandbox/pull/1
As I mentioned before, this functionality can be achieved using cgroups. PRs are welcome.

Thank you. I have prepared a PR with some help from AI. https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/pull/273

## Summary

The `Build network-agent` job in `Build Check` fails on master with `go: updates to go.mod needed` because PR #199 bumped `CubeNet/cubevs` deps without re-tidying its consumers that pull it in via `replace`.

## Environment

- CubeSandbox version / commit: b2eade2625 (master, run [25713548621](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/actions/runs/25713548621/job/75498632236))
- Host OS and kernel version: GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-latest` runner (CI environment)
- KVM info (`modinfo kvm`): N/A — failure is at `go build`, before any KVM interaction
- Deployment mode: N/A — CI build failure
- Relevant component: network-agent (build tooling / module graph)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out master at b2eade2625 (or any commit ≥ a661176115 / PR #199).
2. Build the network-agent builder image and run the `network-agent` build target, e.g.:
   ```bash
   make builder-image
   make builder-run      BUILDER_IMAGE="cube-sandbox-builder:ci"      BUILDER_CMD="mkdir -p /workspace/_output/bin &&                   cd /workspace/network-agent &&                   make proto &&                   go build -o /workspace/_output/bin/network-agent ./cmd/network-agent"
   ```
3. Alternatively, with a Go 1.23+ toolchain locally:
   ```bash
   cd network-agent
   go mod tidy -diff   # exits non-zero, listing the missing entries
   ```

## Expected Behavior

`go build ./cmd/network-agent` produces `_output/bin/network-agent` and the CI job succeeds, as it did on the run for commit 6ce4ddba (run [25657770395](https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/actions/runs/25657770395)).

## Actual Behavior

`go build` aborts with the following (last lines of the failed job log):

```
go: downloading google.golang.org/genproto/googleapis/rpc v0.0.0-20251202230838-ff82c1b0f217
...
go: downloading golang.org/x/text v0.32.0
go: updates to go.mod needed; to update it:
        go mod tidy
make: *** [Makefile:85: builder-run] Error 1
##[error]Process completed with exit code 2.
```

### Root cause

PR #199 (a661176115, "CubeVS: Bump go to 1.24.8, golang.org/x/sys to v0.38.0") changed `CubeNet/cubevs/go.mod`:

| Field | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `go` directive | 1.22 | 1.24.8 |
| `golang.org/x/sys` | v0.30.0 | v0.38.0 |

`network-agent/go.mod` consumes cubevs via local replace:

```
replace github.com/tencentcloud/CubeSandbox/CubeNet/cubevs => ../CubeNet/cubevs
```

Because of the replace, cubevs's go.mod is part of network-agent's effective module graph. PR #199 only ran `go mod tidy` inside `CubeNet/cubevs/`, so `network-agent/go.mod` and `network-agent/go.sum` are now stale relative to the real import graph, and `go build` refuses to proceed.

### Why this slipped through PR-time CI

- `build-check.yml` filters jobs by changed paths, so PR #199 only ran the `cubevs` job — never the `network-agent` job.
- The last commit to actually touch `network-agent/` (6ce4ddba, IPAM refactor on 2026-05-07) was merged before #199, and at that time cubevs deps were still on the old versions, so its build was clean.
- PR #200 was the first push after #199 that triggered the `network-agent` job, so the failure surfaces against #200's commit despite being unrelated to it.

## Additional Context

### Suggested fix

```bash
cd network-agent
go mod tidy
git add go.mod go.sum
git commit -s -m "chore(network-agent): tidy go.sum after cubevs dep bump in #199"
```

Other modules that `replace` cubevs / cubelog (`Cubelet/`, `CubeMaster/`, `agent/`, …) likely have the same latent skew and should be tidied in the same PR even if their CI jobs have not failed yet.

### Prevention

1. Whenever a shared module like `cubevs` or `cubelog` changes its `go.mod`, run `go mod tidy` in **every consumer that replaces it locally**, in the same PR.
2. Add `go mod tidy -diff` to the `builder-run` step (or as a standalone CI step) so this kind of skew fails fast with a clear message instead of being buried 200 lines into a `go build` log.
3. (Stretch) Consider unifying the multi-module repo with a `go.work` file so intra-repo dep changes propagate to consumers' build graphs automatically.

### Related

- PR #199 — root-cause change: https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/pull/199
- PR #200 — first commit to surface the failure: https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/pull/200
- Failing job: https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/actions/runs/25713548621/job/75498632236
- Last green run on `network-agent`: https://github.com/TencentCloud/CubeSandbox/actions/runs/25657770395

Hi @chenggui53,

Thanks for the suggestion! PRs are welcome.

We did consider auto-templating on newly joined nodes. However, one concern is that if the number of templates grows large, it would lead to significant storage consumption across nodes.

Currently, the `cubemastercli tpl` subcommand supports creating templates on a specific node — you can designate a particular template to be built on a newly added compute node, which gives more fine-grained control over storage usage.

If we were to implement auto-templating on new nodes, the storage management aspect would need careful design. We'd love to hear your thoughts on how to handle this — feel free to discuss!

## Proposed Design for Issue #182

@chenggui53 @fslongjin

To address the manual preheating pain after adding new nodes, and to directly tackle the storage concern @fslongjin raised, here's the proposed design:

Add a **preheat controller** in CubeMaster that automatically distributes declared templates onto matching nodes, bounded by explicit storage budgets — no blind full replication.

### Core Decisions

**1. Incremental preheat, operator-declared**
No copying every template to every new node. Operators declare which templates to preheat (`pinned templates`) in config, each with a `node_selector` (label-based matching), `min_replicas` (floor), and `max_replicas` (ceiling). The controller only fills these declared templates.

**2. Hard storage budgets**
Two per-node caps: template count (`per_node_max_templates`) and total bytes (`per_node_max_bytes`). Template size is read from the authoritative source (MySQL). When a budget is exhausted, lower-priority templates are skipped. This is the direct answer to the storage concern — preheat is fully controllable and explainable.

**3. New-node event trigger + periodic backstop**
Preheat fires immediately on node registration, label change, and health transition (low latency); plus a long-interval periodic tick as a backstop for missed events, heartbeat-borne label changes, and cross-master eventual consistency. A newly added node gets a response in seconds, not after waiting for the next poll.

**4. Reuse the existing template distribution path**
No second distribution system. The controller calls the same interface that `cubemastercli tpl redo` uses (`SubmitRedoTemplateFromImage`), reusing its mature distribution, deduplication, and replica-creation logic. The controller only decides *what to fill*; execution is delegated to the existing path.

**5. Non-invasive + disabled by default**
- Does not block node registration, heartbeats, or sandbox scheduling — preheat is purely background and async.
- A preheat failure never marks a node unhealthy and never fails unrelated sandbox creation.
- In multi-CubeMaster deployments, a `GET_LOCK` ensures only one master runs the preheat at a time.
- Defaults to `enabled: false`; the operator must explicitly enable it and declare templates before anything happens.

### TL;DR

A controller — periodic / event-driven — computes "which templates should have replicas on which nodes but don't yet," calls the existing interface to fill the gap, constrained by operator-declared pinned templates and storage budgets, and auto-responds when a new node joins. This removes the manual work while keeping storage consumption entirely in the operator's hands.

---

Feedback welcome, especially on the `min_replicas` / `max_replicas` semantics, sensible budget defaults, and whether to later support automatic template selection by usage heat (deferred to a follow-up). PR ready.

## Problem / Motivation
CubeSandbox sandbox adopts the MicroVM container model with dual-layer virtualization isolation, which enables good reuse and compatibility with the existing K8s Kata container ecosystem.
However, E2B Infra uses a pure MicroVM model. It is architecturally more lightweight, offers more flexible permissions and application ecology inside the sandbox, and can more easily evolve to support heterogeneous OS application ecosystems in the future, such as Windows sandbox and ultra-lightweight LibOS sandbox like Unikraft.
Currently there is no unified support for both two models, limiting ecological compatibility and lightweight sandbox evolution capability.

## Proposed Solution
Support the pure MicroVM model natively on the basis of retaining and being compatible with the existing MicroVM container model of CubeSandbox.
Enable the platform to run both dual-layer virtualization MicroVM container mode and lightweight pure MicroVM mode simultaneously, to accommodate flexible permission management, richer application ecology and heterogeneous OS scenarios including Windows and LibOS sandboxes.

## Alternatives Considered
1. Only keep the existing MicroVM container model: Cannot leverage the lightweight advantage of pure MicroVM, and lacks the flexibility to expand heterogeneous OS and LibOS sandbox ecology.
2. Fully switch to pure MicroVM model: Will lose compatibility with the mature K8s Kata container ecosystem and bring migration cost to existing workloads.

## Bug Description

`GET /v2/sandboxes?state=paused` returns an empty array even when paused sandboxes exist and are visible via the detail endpoint (`GET /sandboxes/<id>`).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a sandbox and pause it:
```bash
curl -sX POST "http://localhost:3000/sandboxes" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"templateID\":\"e2b-code-interpreter\",\"timeout\":300,\"autoPause\":false,\"metadata\":{},\"envVars\":{},\"secure\":true,\"allowInternetAccess\":true}"
# Note the sandboxID

curl -sX POST "http://localhost:3000/sandboxes/<id>/pause"
# Wait ~10s for state transition
```

2. Query paused sandboxes:
```bash
curl -s "http://localhost:3000/v2/sandboxes?state=paused"
# Returns: []   <-- BUG
```

3. Verify the sandbox actually exists and is paused:
```bash
curl -s "http://localhost:3000/sandboxes/<id>" | jq .state
# Returns: "paused"
```

4. Interestingly, combined filter works:
```bash
curl -s "http://localhost:3000/v2/sandboxes?state=paused,running"
# Returns the paused sandbox correctly
```

## Expected Behavior

`GET /v2/sandboxes?state=paused` should return all sandboxes currently in the `paused` state.

## Actual Behavior

- `state=paused` (alone): returns **empty array**
- `state=paused,running` (combined): **works correctly**, paused sandboxes are included
- `GET /sandboxes/<id>` (detail): correctly shows `state: "paused"`
- v1 `GET /sandboxes?state=paused`: same issue

## Impact

- Cannot discover paused sandboxes through the list API
- Operations tooling (batch cleanup, metrics collection, timeout reclamation) cannot find paused instances
- Combined with the state-field misreporting issue (list reports paused as running), paused sandboxes become completely invisible through list endpoints

## Environment

- CubeSandbox latest (master branch)
- Tested on 2026-05-11

## Workaround

Use `state=paused,running` combined filter, then client-side filter by checking each sandbox's detail endpoint for the true state.

Hi @shuaixy,

The root cause is that `--probe 49983` only verifies the `envd` daemon is healthy, but does **not** ensure the code-interpreter gateway on port `49999` is actually up and ready when the template transitions to READY state.

**Fix:** Change your template creation command to probe port `49999` instead:

```bash
cubemastercli template create-from-image \
  --image cube-sandbox-image.tencentcloudcr.com/demo/e2b-code-interpreter:v1.1-data \
  --writable-layer-size 1Gi \
  --template-id e2b-code-interpreter \
  --expose-port 49983 \
  --expose-port 49999 \
  --probe 49999
```

With `--probe 49999`, the template readiness check will wait until the code-interpreter HTTP gateway is actually listening before marking the template as ready. This ensures that when `sandbox.runCode()` is called (which hits `POST :49999/execute`), the service is available and the port mapping is correctly registered in CubeProxy.

We will update the documentation examples to reflect this. Thanks for reporting!
